entry.title: Is a $200 coffee still a little treat?
entry.summary: Plus, the hardcore roots of your hoodie and a house that moved across France in pieces.
entry.content:
Plus, the hardcore roots of your hoodie and a house that moved across France in pieces.

Internet Microdoses

New York to London in 3.5 hours? Not so fast. Boom Supersonic promised a jet that could fly overseas in half the current time. Passengers were expected in the air by 2029, but United's CEO says that's not happening. The airline agreed to conditionally buy 15 jets, but Boom hasn't completed a single prototype of the passenger jet.

Please remain seated →

Three of the world's biggest modern art museums are teaming up. MoMA in New York, the Centre Pompidou in Paris and M+ in Hong Kong will put on exhibitions together and share their collections. Together they attract 10 million visitors a year: think of it as the art world's biggest group project.

Three cities, one alliance →

Could the right apartment cure your loneliness? Frank Lloyd Wright warned that cities were making us feel isolated nearly 100 years ago. Now, architects are rethinking how we live together. Some have designed building has shared balconies, communal dining rooms, and have cheaper rent for young folks who help their older neighbors. Maybe the problem really does start at home.

Meet the neighbors →

Part of London's Oxford Street just banned cars. On October 26, more than half a mile of the tourist destination closed to cars, buses, taxis and bikes, 10 years after the mayor first promised it. Finally, window-shopping without having to dodge a double-decker.

Take a walk →

Someone moved a 1950s house to the other end of France. Designed by Claude Prouvé using his father Jean's construction system, the house was built with factory-made parts. When it was about to be torn down, a collector took it apart and rebuilt it among olive trees in the south. Flat-pack furniture could never.

Book a stay →

A Kandinsky painting has gone up nearly 100,000% in value. In 1964, the Guggenheim was making space and sold Betonte Ecken to a New York dealer for just $62,000. On November 17, Christie’s expects that exact canvas to fetch between $60 million and $80 million. This is why you should never throw anything out.

See the one that got away →

entry.title: Atiba Jefferson
entry.summary: Your favorite skater’s favorite photographer talks Virgil Abloh, mango with almonds, and the case for being nice.
entry.content:
Your favorite skater’s favorite photographer talks Virgil Abloh, mango with almonds, and the case for being nice.

Atiba Jefferson found his place in skateboarding by photographing the people he'd been skating with for years. More than 30 years later, he's your favorite skater's favorite photographer. He's a staff photographer for Thrasher, but his influence spreads wider than the skate scene. He's photographed the Lakers and hangs out with everyone from Turnstile to Tim Robinson. A true alternative icon, he just dropped his second collection with Vans. Here, he shares his case for being nice, why Virgil Abloh inspires him, and his love of mango with almonds.

Can you tell us more about your creative process?

As a photographer, I’m inspired as soon as I open my eyes. I can’t turn off wanting to take photos.

What’s your hot take?

There is no excuse for people to be mean or rude.

Three places you’ve felt inspired by.

Any skate spot, basketball game or concert that I go to.

What do you listen to on repeat?

Turnstile.

What are the most worthwhile investments you’ve made?

Hard work is the best payoff, but also Saint Archer, a beer company I invested in.

What is an unusual habit, or an absurd thing, that you love?

I like the combo of mango and almonds.

Who is your forever inspo?

Virgil Abloh is a huge inspiration to me; he broke every rule.

Write us a fortune cookie message.

Be nice.

entry.title: The Corner 022
entry.summary: After years in front of the camera, a model decides how much of his face to show.
entry.content:
After years in front of the camera, a model decides how much of his face to show.

Sang Woo Kim's The Corner 022 (2026) is a self-portrait cropped so close that only half his face fits: one eye, the side of his nose, half his mouth and an ear. He painted the skin in oil and acrylic, mixing ochre, orange and tan with a little green and gray. Kim was born in Seoul in 1994 and moved to Britain as a child. He lives in London, and in May his work was shown in Venice during the Biennale.

Growing up, he was one of very few Asian kids in his school and faced racial discrimination, with bullies focusing on the shape of his eyes. Later, working as a model, he saw the fashion industry fetishize the same feature. Now, he’s reclaiming his features as the focus of his own work. In a 2024 artist statement, he made his intentions clear: “As I become more of myself – the artist – the more I intend to reveal of my face, body, autonomy.”

entry.title: Everything is hardcore
entry.summary: How the hoodies, work pants, and sneakers worn in mosh pits and on skate ramps became an everyday uniform.
entry.content:
How the hoodies, work pants, and sneakers worn in mosh pits and on skate ramps became an everyday uniform.

A gray Champion hoodie, Adidas track pants or Dickies workwear, Vans or a pair of Jordans, and a varsity jacket for when it's cold out. That’s the default outfit you throw on to run errands, do laundry, or lie around your living room all Sunday.

But forty years ago, that look was also a uniform for the misfits. In the mid-'80s, a scene of New York hardcore kids showed up to shows dressed for gym class, starting a movement that would be known as youth crew. In California, pro skaters were throwing themselves down ramps in similar fits.

For most of us, this outfit feels like a nice neutral when we don't want to overthink. But the true heads in our midst know the hardcore and skate history stitched into it.

entry.title: Would you tattoo your hair?
entry.summary: People are painting their heads and stripping copper wire on TikTok. And the world keeps spinning.
entry.content:
People are painting their heads and stripping copper wire on TikTok. And the world keeps spinning.

Internet Microdoses

TikTok’s latest trend is stripping copper wire. Copper prices hit a record this year, so creators peel the plastic off old cables and sell the metal inside as scrap. One woman filmed herself doing it for six months to save for a house. She says the copper earned her $99, while a video about it earned her $1,446. Somewhere, a scrapyard owner is buying a ring light. Strip for the algorithm →

You can now get an official Rembrandt tattoo. Amsterdam's Rembrandt House Museum has opened a pop-up tattoo studio. Walk-ins can get a small Rembrandt design for as little as $110. One volunteer is getting The Descent from the Cross across his whole back, which takes about 20 hours. Exit through the tattoo shop →

Apple Music's new logo was made by sound. For its first rebrand since 2015, Apple and Fred again.. played sound frequencies into a shallow pool of oil. The ripples distorted the logo, creating its new visual identity. And to think they used to use computers, like cavemen. Turn it up →

Mexico’s archaeology institute has identified a 2,500-year-old solar observatory. Archaeologists say the platforms at Tetelihtic, in central Mexico, were built to track where the sun rises. The alignments may have marked the start of the year in February and harvest time in October. But how did they turn it back for daylight saving time? Watch the sun come up →

The first episode of an AI-generated Odyssey made with Elon Musk's Grok has been released, and everyone’s roasting it. After criticizing Christopher Nolan's casting, Musk promised his AI tool Grok would make a "historically accurate" version of Homer's epic. Seven minutes into Elon’s, Nolan's is starting to look like a documentary. Set sail, if you dare →

Ibrahim Mahama moved part of a Ghanaian glass factory to Paris. The bottle factory opened in 1966, weeks before Ghana's first president was overthrown, and was about to be scrapped. Mahama bought it and rebuilt a section inside the Fondation Cartier, surrounded by more than 25,000 green glass bottles. Talk about bottle service →

entry.title: Jackie
entry.summary: A towering beaded jack-o’-lantern with precious stones forming the rot inside.
entry.content:
A towering beaded jack-o’-lantern with precious stones forming the rot inside.

Kathleen Ryan's Jackie (2021) is a jack-o'-lantern with its lid tipped over on the floor beside it. The skin is studded with tens of thousands of acrylic beads. The rot inside is lapis, malachite, amethyst, and agate, pinned on by hand. She usually saves the cheap beads for the fresh parts and the real stones for the decay, so the moldiest bit is worth the most. It stands over 5 feet tall.

Ryan was born in Santa Monica in 1984 and minored in archaeology. Before grad school, she coordinated Jeff Koons's plastics projects at the fabricator Carlson & Co. Her Bad Fruit series started in 2018 with beaded plastic fruit she found in thrift stores. Jackie is now in the Nasher Sculpture Center's collection in Dallas. Its grin gives a view of the rot inside.

entry.title: Hair lines
entry.summary: From towering ship hairstyles to bleached headphones, a history of wearing your identity in your hair.
entry.content:
From towering ship hairstyles to bleached headphones, a history of wearing your identity in your hair.

April Harper Grey is best known as underscores, one of the biggest names in hyperpop, a genre of experimental electronic pop music. The 26-year-old singer and producer released her third album, U, in March, and this fall she's opening for Charli XCX in arenas. You can recognize her by her hair: dark, with the outline of a pair of headphones bleached into it. Her fans are recreating the design on their own heads.

People have worn symbols in their hair to show what they believe in or who they admire for centuries. In 1778, after a French frigate (a warship) fought a British ship, women at the French court in Versailles built model ships into hairstyles up to two feet high.

Since then, people have dyed, shaved, and bleached everything from AIDS ribbons to Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper into their hair.

entry.title: Adriana Roslin
entry.summary: A Madrid-born photographer and creative director creating minimal, architectural images shaped by light.
entry.content:
A Madrid-born photographer and creative director creating minimal, architectural images shaped by light.

Adriana Roslin starts every shoot by finding the right light. The Madrid-born creative director and photographer chooses locations for how light falls across their surfaces. Her minimal, almost architectural images have appeared in Vogue Spain and GQ Spain. Her clients include Loewe, Adidas, and Spotify. Right now, she's juggling a shoe campaign, a project for the Spanish airline Iberia, and a documentary. Here, Adriana shares her case against Instagram, the best investments she's made, and the airport pat-down videos that give her ASMR.

What's your hot take?

Instagram has become this major dystopian TV screen that feeds our insecurities, our anger, and our despair. We are constantly forced to witness the misuse of power by influencers and celebrities who are, whether we like it or not, a big pillar of contemporary “culture.” They are there, and companies and fans continue to give them massive platforms. We are also forced to consume an overwhelming amount of completely different content within a matter of seconds, in a way that our brains simply cannot fully process. And especially now, it feels more intense than ever. Instagram has also pushed us to limit ourselves creatively, stopping artists from experimenting with their images because of censorship, changing the crops and formats of our work to fit a standard, and making us feel that we should be doing what everyone else is doing simply because it worked for them and the brands they might be working for. We need healthier options so we stop destroying our mental health.

Three places you’ve felt inspired by.

Anywhere with good natural light coming through, anywhere with a sunset, and anywhere with interesting interiors.

What do you listen to on repeat?

Right now, “Uno” by Ben Yart.

What are the most worthwhile investments you've made?

Good accountants, a cheaper but better living space even if it’s further away from the city centre, and an emotionally stable partner.

What is an unusual habit, or an absurd thing, that you love?

I watch a lot of YouTube videos of doctors giving medical exams, people inspecting rooms, and airport pat-downs. They give me ASMR.

Tell us more about your creative process.

For me, something that is very inspiring is always my surroundings, especially how the light might affect certain surfaces in them. That’s why, when I think about a shoot, I immediately think about the location and what it could give us that could benefit artistically. And then I go from there.

Who is your forever inspo?

Sonia Szostak. She is a great photographer. She really knows how to blend in any situation and always creates something interesting.

Write us a fortune cookie.

Try to live any experience as positively as possible because almost everything is surmountable. With the right support and vibes, you will do it. Also, life is too short.

entry.title: Does this make my brain look big?
entry.summary: Books are having a great year. Reading is another story.
entry.content:
Books are having a great year. Reading is another story.

Internet Microdoses

Elizabeth Holmes is selling out cinemas. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s three-hour You Can See Everything made $15 million and sold out more than 2,000 showings in its opening weekend. That’s the biggest documentary debut in two decades, excluding music and concert films. Finally, she’s attached to a product that delivers. Cue the black turtlenecks this Halloween →

Tiny lab-grown brains can now tell Braille letters apart. Researchers turned Braille letters into electrical signals and fed them to clumps of human brain cells, each smaller than a millimeter. One clump got 61% right, while three working together got 83%. Sometimes you really do just need to rub a couple of brain cells together. Meet the brains in a dish →

The world's new contender just turned up near Turkey. The boat rotted away long ago, but divers found more than 30 clay jars and three stone anchors from up to 4,700 years ago, when Egypt's first pyramids were going up. Some jars still held residue, likely olive oil or wine. Dive in →

Arsenal’s font took four years to design. With tens of millions of fans, designer David Rudnick thought the football club deserved a hype-worthy typeface. He hand-drew Rocastle, a spiky Old English font named after the legendary David Rocastle, for everything from jerseys to fashion collabs. The G alone took about 2,000 redraws. What a G →

France’s protests have reached the Louvre. Students from the École du Louvre blocked the museum’s entrance on Monday, joining nationwide demonstrations over the cost of living. What started as demands for better school conditions has brought roughly half a million people into the streets across France. Behind the blockade →

Maine has its own Sistine Chapel. From the outside, the South Solon Meeting House is a plain white New England church. Inside, nearly every wall is covered in 1950s frescoes, including a Great Flood modeled on Michelangelo's. Let yourself in →

Sasha Gordon's Hard Candies (2026) is a portrait of a green woman admiring a translucent paperweight. Gordon builds her paintings from thin, translucent layers of oil, so the skin glows. She graduated from RISD in 2020. Her work is now in The Broad’s collection, and David Zwirner began co-representing her in 2024. Hard Candies hangs in Nocturnal at Zwirner Hong Kong through November 14.

Gordon often paints herself, using her body as what Zwirner calls "a kind of unorthodox avatar." Hard Candies is a rare exception: the sitter is someone else, peering into a crystal paperweight that belonged to Gordon's grandmother: a glass egg holding a tiny garden of red caps, orange toadstools, and a teal flower. It's an object inside a painting about loving an object.

Look closely, and she's doing exactly what you're doing right now.

entry.title: Turning the page
entry.summary: Books are on the runway, on your bag, and arranged by color. Reading them is optional.
entry.content:
Books are on the runway, on your bag, and arranged by color. Reading them is optional.

Now more than ever, books are props. Last year, the internet couldn't stop arguing about "performative reading" on the subway and at the bar, as if doomscrolling were better. Coach and Penguin Random House turned real books into bag charms. Alix Earle told Interview she’d never read a book, then offered “maybe Dr. Seuss.” The internet didn’t like that. Apparently, there’s a wrong way not to read, too.

In a 2025 Gallup survey, 43% of Gen Z students said they rarely or never read for fun.

Yes, the book is having a great year, even if no one's reading it.

entry.title: Drew Michael Scott
entry.summary: Lone Fox’s Drew Michael Scott on vintage finds, trusting his eye, and opening a store against advice.
entry.content:
Lone Fox’s Drew Michael Scott on vintage finds, trusting his eye, and opening a store against advice.

Drew Michael Scott wants your home to look like you found every object in it yourself. The Lone Fox founder fills rooms with vintage pieces, old design books, and objects with a past, mixing eras until a space feels complete. His third collection with Joon Loloi just launched. This time he went with his gut: animal print, patchwork, borders, and a little Gothic, which he thinks will surprise people. Here, he shares the Parma vintage market that inspires him, the Fortuny lamps he can't stop researching, and the advice he proudly ignored about opening a store.

Can you tell us more about your creative process?

My creative process is really about finding inspiration in unexpected places and allowing myself to experiment. I’m drawn to vintage pieces, old design books, and objects with history because they bring a sense of character and individuality that you can’t always find in something new. I love mixing different eras, textures, and styles to create something that feels collected rather than overly designed. I also think it’s important to trust your own eye and not get too caught up in trends. My style has evolved so much over the years, and some of my best ideas come from being open to where the process takes me!

Three places you’ve felt inspired by. (City, space, park, museum, restaurant, corner store, club)

  1. Printemps in New York City.
  2. Stockholm, Sweden: there’s so much inspiration in the architecture, and Swedish design is some of my favorite.
  3. The vintage market Mercanteinfiera in Parma, Italy.

What’s an item you can’t live without?

A hat because I don’t like to do my hair every day!

What song are you listening to on repeat?

I’ve really been loving Slayyyter's and Remi Wolf's new albums!

What can't you stop thinking about and why?

I’ve been doing a lot of research on Fortuny fabric and lights. The craftsmanship is so interesting, and I love the elevation it adds to the space.

Who is your forever inspo?

Kelly Wearstler: she’s been able to create an empire and has such individual style. I love her fashion and interiors. It’s inspiring how she scaled her business and has become such a household name.

Write us a fortune cookie.

You’re the only one who can make yourself into something.

entry.summary: In Japan, they are. Plus shipwreck chic and what might be the first mirror selfie ever.
entry.content:
In Japan, they are. Plus shipwreck chic and what might be the first mirror selfie ever.

Internet Microdoses

Getty Images plans to file for bankruptcy after spending $100 million on a $3.7 billion merger with Shutterstock that didn’t pan out. Now it's going private with help from Charles Koch's investment firm. With AI making generic stock photos easy to fake, Getty will focus on red carpets and real news. Say cheese (for now) →

Finally, a rave for people who’d rather be reading. Tokyo’s SPREAD carpeted its dance floor, played ambient music, and let people lie around with books. Everyone’s getting lit with literature. BYOB: bring your own book →

Virginia Woolf’s grandmother may have taken one of the original mirror selfie. The V&A has acquired Mia Jackson’s late-1850s self-portrait, possibly the earliest deliberate mirror selfie. Cameras had no timers back then, so someone stood behind her to pull the lens cap. And she still managed to serve →

A moodboard icon is having trouble finding a buyer. The Stahl House, a glass-walled LA landmark, was listed for $25 million last November, but buyers balked at only two bedrooms and restrictions on expansion. If you’ve got one roommate and $20 million between you, go check it out →

Your next pitch deck could use a little Michelangelo. Created by studiogusto for the 400th anniversary of the consecration of St. Peter’s Basilica, the Michelangelus font arrives in Word at the end of the year. Can’t wait to see how this looks on “bathrooms are for customers only” signs. Still beats Comic Sans →

An ode to the burner account, thanks to Channing Tatum. The Magic Mike hunk was accused of using a secret Instagram to roast his ex, Zoë Kravitz. He denies it was his, but now others are fessing up about their finstas. Read the stalkers’ confessions →

entry.summary: A visual inspiration platform for creatives — save, organize, search, and discover images, links, videos, articles, and text in a distraction-free, ad-free environment.
entry.content:
A visual inspiration platform for creatives — save, organize, search, and discover images, links, videos, articles, and text in a distraction-free, ad-free environment.

Polina Osipova's Sliding towards the ancient (2026) is a pink felt rocket ship with a playground slide coming out of it. Osipova is a self-taught artist from the Indigenous Chuvash people of central Russia. Her pearl headpieces and silver coin headdresses went viral before she turned 25. She’s since had solo shows in London, New York, and now Berlin, where this piece lives at Neun Kelche. Her sculptures often use old family photos. Here, they're covered in thin metal plates, the way Orthodox icons are.

In Chuvash belief, people become stars when they die. Soviet playgrounds taught kids that space was something to conquer. Osipova's rocket heads the other way, toward the ancestors. Down the slide, it reads: "Voyage towards the ancient, I take my place in the sun." And yes, you're allowed to ride it.

entry.title: Shipwrecked
entry.summary: A castaway in 1866 sewed her own sealskin outfit to survive. 160 years later, Chanel is selling the look.
entry.content:
A castaway in 1866 sewed her own sealskin outfit to survive. 160 years later, Chanel is selling the look.

Ask anyone how they’re doing, and you’ll likely hear some version of “just trying to stay afloat” or “barely keeping my head above water.” It’s no wonder we’re all dressing like we just survived a shipwreck.

In 1866, Mary Ann Jewell was stranded in the sub-Antarctic after her ship went down. For 18 months, she survived in clothes she sewed from sealskin using needles carved from albatross bone.

Her ship sank with a fortune in gold aboard. But Mary Ann returned with something that earned her an unexpected payday. Now Chanel is selling her shipwreck aesthetic 160 years later.

entry.title: Kat Irlin
entry.summary: The photographer behind fashion's chicest covers, where every shoot starts with a crush.
entry.content:
The photographer behind fashion's chicest covers, where every shoot starts with a crush.

Kat Irlin traded finance for art. After ten years in the corporate world, she switched to photography and now shoots campaigns for some of the most illustrious brands and covers for the chicest magazines. Her process starts with a crush: a model, a shoe, a ring, or a city catches her eye, and she builds a whole story around it. Here, she shares more on her favorite music and why kindness is her hot take.

Can you tell us more about your creative process?

All forms of beauty inspire me: people, places, things. I get interested in a subject and build a story around it, aiming to show it to the world in a way it hasn’t been seen before. I love bringing out the best in whoever or whatever I’m shooting. With people, that means connecting with them and making them feel comfortable and at ease. That’s when they shine.

Three places you've felt inspired by.

  1. New York, always.
  2. Anywhere with a beautiful interior.
  3. Anywhere with beautiful light.

What's your hot take?

Kindness is everything.

What do you listen to on repeat?

The most random mix of music from all over the world, from the 1950s to now.

What is the most worthwhile investment you've made?

My kids — they are kind, smart and hardworking! My work — always taking the time to put the best stuff out there that stands out.

What is an unusual habit, or an absurd thing, that you love?

I love looking at vintage jewelry for hours :)

Who is your forever inspo?

The beauty in everything.

Write us a fortune cookie.

Create and prosper!

Katherine Gray’s shallow glass bowl runs from lavender to teal to sapphire to near-black, and the colors move when you do. Sandblasted to a fine, sandy matte, it’s coated in microscopically thin layers of metallic oxide and vaporized quartz — a NASA process Gray borrowed to shrink a James Turrell light field down to something you can cup in two hands.

Gray knows glass. A Canadian who took her MFA at RISD, she teaches glass at Cal State San Bernardino and judges Netflix’s Blown Away, and her work is in the Corning Museum of Glass. She knows the material well enough to make it do anything. Here, the bowl is flushed and poreless and warm to the eye. The color never quite settles anywhere you can point to. Tilt it, and the blue has already moved on.

entry.title: Irresistible Reversibles
entry.summary: Reversibles promise you'll own less, but no one can stop buying them.
entry.content:
Reversibles promise you'll own less, but no one can stop buying them.

Reversible coats have been saving people money for centuries — and occasionally their lives. Shepherds wore a warm side and a cool side.

The MA-1 bomber, later the most bootlegged jacket in streetwear, was reversible on purpose: sage green on the outside, a panel of bright orange inside that downed pilots turned out so rescue crews could spot them.

Two-for-one has always had obvious appeal when budgets are thin, and these revivals tend to land in exactly those years.

So it's no wonder reversibles are back as the sleeper outerwear story of the fall. They promise to help us own less, but we can’t seem to stop buying them.

entry.title: Thom Bettridge
entry.summary: The magazine whisperer turning print institutions into internet-native brands.
entry.content:
The magazine whisperer turning print institutions into internet-native brands.

Thom Bettridge is the guy magazines call when they need saving. Over the past decade he's taken some of fashion and culture's best-known titles — Interview, Highsnobiety, and most recently i-D — and rebuilt each so that they serve people who grew up online without losing their print prestige. As a side quest, he ran the creative side of the luxury retailer SSENSE. Up next, he's launching his creative studio CONTENT WORLD. Here, he tells us why reality TV is secretly one of our best art forms, why he's handed his aux over to the radio, and why he thinks "community" has become the most misused word around.

Three places you've felt inspired by.

  1. My office (coworkers get me inspired)
  2. Louvre Lens (incredible architecture)
  3. Walking through Central Park (always and forever)

What's your hot take?

I think one of the great paradoxes of our cultural moment is contained within the word "Community," something that we all need, but at the same time, the way we use the word is almost always wrong. Liking the same thing is not a "community." Waiting on line for the same brunch or concert is not a "community." Communities are groups that share tangible ideals and contribute concretely to each other, whether that be materially, socially, or emotionally.

What do you listen to on repeat?

I've recently gotten into listening to the radio, so I can't repeat songs (or even have a choice of what I'm listening to). My favorite is WKCR, which is the Columbia University station (89.9 FM if you’re in New York City).

What is the most worthwhile investment you've made?

Making student publications while I was in college. It was the perfect training ground for making magazines and probably more valuable than the classes I paid tuition for.

What is an unusual habit, or an absurd thing, that you love?

I don't like scripted or "prestige" television, but I love watching reality television. It's a near-perfect art form filled with unreal levels of comedy, pathos, and social satire. The way that we read plays to understand ancient Greece, people in the future will watch reality shows to understand our society.

Who is your forever inspo?

I have so many, but will name a few... people who made "Content" before the internet existed like George Lois, Oliviero Toscani, or even Andy Kaufman. Film directors who are masters of world-building like Kubrick, Rohmer, or Miyazaki.

Write us a fortune cookie message.

Don't take the bait, savor it.

Joyce Lin's table and chair are antiquities sealed away. Each block of matte blue acrylic suspends a blurred antique just out of reach. Lin is a Houston-based artist and furniture maker who treats familiar forms like chairs and tables as studies in dissection and mimicry. She studied furniture design at RISD and geology-biology at Brown; for this 2019 exhibition, she collaborated with Emeric Tchatchoua of the fashion label 3.Paradis on a series about dreams and remembrance.

The series was called “For Now We See Through A Glass Darkly,” which comes from 1 Corinthians 13:12 — a biblical banger about trying and failing to see what the future holds. Here, Lin looks back. The chair is a tufted comfort, evoking a weekend at Grandma’s. But it’s completely off-limits and forever out of reach.

entry.title: Faking Fall
entry.summary: The season we build because we can no longer count on the one we're given.
entry.content:
The season we build because we can no longer count on the one we're given.

Stars Hollow was never in Connecticut. They shot Gilmore Girls on a backlot in Burbank, where the crew faked New England autumn by swapping real leaves for silk ones, creating the perfect backdrop for Rory and Lorelai to sip from obviously empty coffee cups.

Twenty-plus years later, the new reigning queen of fall is Caitlin Covington — the de facto spokesperson for “Christian Girl Autumn” — who makes a pilgrimage to Vermont every single year to find the real thing.

Both are forcing it, but it raises the question: Which is the authentic autumn — the one you build or the one you cross the country to stand in?

Terrence Zhou’s flower sits inside a translucent, egg-shaped balloon — hot-pink petals and an acid-green stem, softened by the plastic until they blur, in the colors of a corner-store sweet. Born in China and based in New York, Zhou is the designer behind Bad Binch TongTong, a fashion label known for ballooning dresses, octopus skirts, and mermaid tails. He studied math before fashion, which might explain his mastery of geometric shapes.

Here you can make out the flower but never quite see it. The shell holds it just out of focus, like a specimen you’re not allowed to touch and barely allowed to look at. A clear photograph of a flower is one thing, but this one evokes memory and feeling.

entry.title: Microcinemas
entry.summary: Tiny rooms, mismatched chairs, films too strange to book anywhere else: inside the microcinema revival.
entry.content:
Tiny rooms, mismatched chairs, films too strange to book anywhere else: inside the microcinema revival.

Low Cinema opened last year in a windowless former barber shop in Ridgewood, Queens. It’s the neighborhood’s first new cinema in nearly a hundred years. Inside: 42 secondhand seats, a papier-mâché E.T. that co-founder John Wilson (yes, that John Wilson) made by hand, and a framed counterfeit ticket someone bought off Facebook Marketplace. The ticket scanner beeps on purpose. They had a developer add the sound because a beep reassures people their ticket actually went through.

There are others like it all over the world. Los Angeles went from one and a half microcinemas to five or six almost overnight, by one distributor’s count. In Ridgewood, a couple nailed a bedsheet to a rooftop and called it a theater. In Toronto, video store Eyesore Cinema can seat up to 40 people for its off-kilter programming. The rooms all look alike: mismatched chairs, a popcorn machine, an iPad for a box office, 16mm nights, walls papered in flyers.

Jennifer Crupi studied at Cooper Union and now teaches metalwork at Kean University in New Jersey. Her body of work is all about body language: sterling silver devices that lock you into gestures, working off the idea that holding a pose can make you actually feel it.

Ornamental Hands: Figure One is a set of fine chains and finger braces that hang from a wrist cuff and hold your hand, marionette-style, in one of those elegant poses from old portraits. It works like a splint, getting your fingers to sit just so. It’s in the Smithsonian collection now. Slip it on and your hand looks like it belongs in a painting.

entry.title: Welded Laptop
entry.summary: A visual inspiration platform for creatives — save, organize, search, and discover images, links, videos, articles, and text in a distraction-free, ad-free environment.
entry.content:
A visual inspiration platform for creatives — save, organize, search, and discover images, links, videos, articles, and text in a distraction-free, ad-free environment.

German artist Alexander Endrullat studied architecture at the Bauhaus University before moving into fine art in Dresden, and that way of looking at things stuck. In his work, laptops and tablets become materials: slabs, joints, shells, surfaces — things to bend, crush, or rebuild.

For his series Unibody, Endrullat took Apple’s idea of a laptop machined from a single piece of aluminum to its logical conclusion. He welded the screen to the base, turning the MacBook into a genuinely solid object with no way in.

It still looks totally normal. Better, even. There’s a little seam where the lid meets the base, but this laptop is never opening again. It just gets to be a nice piece of aluminum, and honestly some days that’s all a laptop should be. No notifications or emails to answer. Just a beautiful object on your coffee table.
